title: BLACKPINK's Hit Songwriter Says YG Trapped Her at 18, Forced an Abortion, Paid Her Almost Nothing — 'The Members Did Nothing'
excerpt: Bekuh Boom, the songwriter behind BLACKPINK's biggest global hits including Lisa's 'MONEY', went viral alleging YG Entertainment signed her to a predatory contract at 18 with a fake debut promise, verbally abused her, pressured her to terminate a pregnancy, and paid her a fraction of what her songs earned. BLACKPINK said nothing.
author: MEARROW Editorial Desk
content:
On March 19, a TikTok video turned K-pop's most glittering corner dark.

**Bekuh Boom** — the songwriter behind some of BLACKPINK's most-streamed global hits — sat in front of a camera and began talking. What she said struck at the K-pop industry's most persistent open secret: that behind the chart records and stadium tours, the people who actually write the music are often the most exploited people in the room.

Her allegations against YG Entertainment and, by implication, BLACKPINK's members have since ignited a fierce debate — about industry abuse, about idol power dynamics, and about whether a rival label is quietly pulling the strings.

## Who Is Bekuh Boom?

If you don't know her name, you know her work.

Bekuh Boom co-wrote some of BLACKPINK's defining tracks — **'BOOMBAYAH'**, **'DDU-DU DDU-DU'** — and contributed to Lisa's solo monster **'MONEY'**, which crossed 1.5 billion YouTube views and became one of the highest-streamed K-pop solo tracks ever. She also wrote for JEON SOMI and K/DA, the League of Legends virtual pop group. She was one of a small cohort of American songwriters embedded in the K-pop machine, whose names appeared quietly in the credits while the artists took the stage.

That quiet, she says, was not by choice.

## 'I Was 18. They Promised Me a Debut.'

The central allegation is about a contract.

Bekuh Boom claims that when she was **18 years old**, YG Entertainment signed her with a promise: support for her own debut as a solo artist. What she actually received, she says, was a decade of writing for their artists instead. Her own music career, she claims, was repeatedly deferred, shelved, and ultimately denied while BLACKPINK's discography grew on the back of her work.

On TikTok, she described the period as exploitation — saying the label **"took advantage of her from a young age."** The specific terms of that contract have not been made public. YG Entertainment has issued no response.

One detail from community discussion is worth flagging: some online commenters noted that Bekuh Boom signed with **Warner Chappell** (a publishing company) at 18, raising questions about the specific timeline. Bekuh Boom has not publicly clarified this discrepancy.

![K-pop songwriter Bekuh Boom's YG Entertainment abuse allegations — the darker side of BLACKPINK's global success story](/images/news/bekuh-boom-blackpink-yg-songwriter-abortion-contract-2026-1.webp)

## The Abortion Allegation

The most explosive claim in Bekuh Boom's account is not about money. It is about her body.

She alleges that YG Entertainment **pressured her to terminate a pregnancy**. In K-pop, "no-dating clauses" embedded in idol contracts are widely documented. The idea that such control extended to the pregnancy decisions of a songwriter — not even a signed idol — would mark a significant escalation of the documented range of label overreach.

No evidence beyond Bekuh Boom's own testimony has been presented publicly. YG has not addressed this allegation.

## 'MONEY' and the Royalty Gap

Separately, Bekuh Boom alleges she was **vastly underpaid for Lisa's 'MONEY'**.

'MONEY' is not a minor footnote. It is one of the most commercially successful K-pop solo releases ever recorded — over 1.5 billion views on YouTube, a genuine Western radio crossover, and a staple of every global K-pop metrics discussion. By any standard, it generated substantial revenue. Bekuh Boom's claim is that her share of that revenue did not reflect her contribution.

Songwriter compensation in K-pop — and in much of the global pop industry — has long been a documented problem. Writers frequently receive flat fees rather than royalty participation, and backend earnings from catalog streaming rarely flow proportionally to the people who created the music. If Bekuh Boom's account reflects accurate numbers, it is a specific instance of a structural industry failure.

## 'The Members Did Nothing'

The accusation that landed hardest for fans was not directed at YG.

Bekuh Boom said BLACKPINK's members **provided no support** during her most difficult period with the label. She did not stop there: she **liked a social media comment** that said BLACKPINK should have spoken up for her. In K-pop's hyperattentive fan culture, that like registered as a public statement.

The reaction among BLINKs was immediate and divided. Some acknowledged that BLACKPINK members may themselves have had limited power within YG's hierarchical structure and were not in a position to advocate openly for a songwriter. Others rejected that framing entirely, arguing the members had enough leverage to speak — and chose silence.

It is also documented that Bekuh Boom previously had a public falling-out with Jennie, adding a layer of interpersonal history to what she presents as a systemic critique.

## The HYBE Variable

The timing of Bekuh Boom's viral moment has not gone unnoticed.

She is currently writing songs for **ILLIT**, the girl group under HYBE's BELIFT LAB. The fact that BLACKPINK's former songwriter is now under the HYBE umbrella — and is publicly targeting YG on social media at precisely the moment BTS's ARIRANG is dominating global charts — has generated a significant counter-narrative among BLACKPINK fans.

On social media, the response has been pointed: *"Bekuh Boom is a HYBE employee now. This is a coordinated smear campaign against BLACKPINK and YG."*

It is a logical concern in the context of K-pop's entertainment-industry politics, where label warfare is real and proven. It is also worth noting that writers work across multiple labels all the time, and HYBE employment would not inherently invalidate Bekuh Boom's account of past treatment at YG. Both things can be true.

## What MEARROW Is Watching

Bekuh Boom's allegations are one-sided, unverified, and — so far — unanswered by YG or BLACKPINK. None of that makes them wrong. It makes them unresolved.

Three things stand out in this situation.

**First, the songwriter's compensation structure.** Whether or not every specific allegation holds up, the economic gap between how much revenue BLACKPINK's hits generated and how much Bekuh Boom says she received is worth examining. K-pop's hit machine has a documented pattern of back-loading songwriter compensation into flat fees while the backend value accumulates to labels and artists. That pattern is not unique to YG.

**Second, the limits of idol power.** Blaming BLACKPINK's four members for not defending a songwriter to the company that controlled their careers, their public image, and their financial futures requires a specific theory of how much power those members actually had. The evidence from the broader K-pop industry — including the ADOR/HYBE/NewJeans saga — suggests that even successful groups have limited leverage against their labels when things go wrong.

**Third, HYBE's strategic position.** The optics of YG's star songwriter going public against YG while working for HYBE are difficult to ignore. That doesn't make the story false. But it does mean the full context of these allegations — including what is in Bekuh Boom's interest to say, when, and to whom — matters as much as the content.

Neither BLACKPINK nor YG Entertainment has spoken. Until they do, this story is missing at least half of its evidence. What's already visible is enough to keep the K-pop industry's structural problems front and center — exactly where they have been for years.
